proxy_language: Unidentified: 'Katuirlìunach' is not a known historical culture or language. Best defensible proxy is a hedge: Middle Korean (15th c., Hunmin jeongeum / Hangul-era court register) for an East Asian later court, with Sino-Korean vocabulary for court and ritual terms.
proxy_rationale: The culture label matches no attested East or Southeast Asian polity, and its form (Kat-, -lìunach, grave accent) looks Goidelic or invented rather than East Asian. The region tag and 'later_court' kind suggest a literate bureaucratic court of the later Middle Ages, for which Middle Korean (Yale romanization) offers a well-documented, regular system with native and Sino-Korean strata. The link to the actual culture is essentially nil. Alternatives with equal standing would be Classical Japanese (Heian) or Middle Vietnamese. If the design intent is a fictional Gaelic-flavoured people, that conflicts with the region tag and should be resolved by the studio.
phonology: Middle Korean (Yale romanization). Consonants: p t k c s h m n ng l; tense/aspirated series ph th kh ch; pp tt kk cc ss; z (voiced fricative, native words only); w y glides. Vowels: i e a o wu u (pharyngeal/labial), plus eo/ay/oy/wuy diphthongs. Pitch accent: low (unmarked), high (marked with a dot), rising (two dots); this was written with side-dots in Hunmin jeongeum texts and should not be rendered in names.
phonotactics: Syllable shape (C)(G)V(C). Onset: at most one consonant, optionally with glide y/w. Coda: only p t k m n ng l (written; neutralized to k t p in isolation). No consonant clusters inside the syllable in native words (older texts show clusters like pt, ps, sk only as initial clusters in 15th c.; avoid them). Initial l is rare or absent in native words; initial ng does not occur. Words end in vowel or one of the codas listed. Vowel harmony (bright a o / dark e wu u) operates in suffixes.
orthography: Yale romanization of Middle Korean, in lowercase: digraphs ng, ch, kh, ph, th, pp, tt, kk, ss, cc, eo (as in Yale, written 'e' for the mid-central vowel and 'wu' for the high back unrounded), 'ey', 'ay', 'oy', 'wu', 'yu'. For Sino-Korean court terms use the Yale reading of the character. Hyphens separate morphemes only in glossing, not in names. Words are written solid, with spaces between noun phrase members.
morphology: Agglutinative, SOV, head-final. Nouns have no gender or number marking (plural suffix -tol is optional). Postpositions/case: -i/-ka nominative, -ul/-lul accusative, -uy genitive, -ey locative/dative, -ay (with harmony), -ulo/-ro instrumental, -wa/-kwa 'and'. Verbs take honorific -sywo-/-wusi-, tense -ke-/-e-, nominalizer -um/-m, adnominal -n/-l. Vocabulary has two strata: native roots (mostly 1-2 syllables) and Sino-Korean (SK) monosyllabic morphemes freely combined into 2-4 syllable compounds, which dominate court, ritual, rank and architecture terms.
compounding: Head-final: modifier precedes head. Native N+N compounds juxtapose directly (kulum-san 'cloud mountain'); a sai-sios linking consonant (-s) appears in some compounds (e.g. nay-s-mwul 'stream water'). Genitive 'X of Y' = Y-uy X (Y's X), but SK compounds omit the particle: Y X (e.g. cheyn-kwuk 'heaven-country'). 'Y-maker' type agent names use SK suffix -kong 'artisan' / -sa 'master' or native -i 'person' and -ci 'one who does'. Place names: X-san 'mountain', X-kang 'river', X-sa 'temple', X-cen 'hall', X-kwung 'palace', X-lu 'pavilion'.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier-head: adjective/adnominal clause then noun; genitive noun then head noun; numeral then classifier-less noun in older texts. Demonstratives precede the noun (i 'this', ku 'that', ce 'yonder').

notes: The culture name 'Katuirlìunach' is not an East or Southeast Asian ethnonym and does not match any attested language; the proxy above is a placeholder chosen only to satisfy the region tag, with speculative confidence. The studio should confirm intent before relying on it. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic; the Middle Korean proxy is not Goidelic, so this rule applies in full.
